The checkpoint wasn't pushed because I pushed to the repo URL instead of the remote name `origin`.

Entire stores checkpoints on a separate branch, `entire/checkpoints/v1`. It doesn't put them on your code branch. Its `pre-push` hook (`.git/hooks/pre-push`) pushes that branch whenever you push code, using the remote name that Git passes in as `$1`. I ran `git push https://github.com/migmartri/slacktronic.git …` to follow your HTTPS rule, so the hook got a URL instead of a remote name. It skipped the checkpoint push without showing an error.

| `entire/checkpoints/v1` | Commit | Has checkpoint `02cdc0f5c85b`? |
|---|---|---|
| Local | `bb1804d` (Finalize transcript for Checkpoint: 02cdc0f5c85b) | Yes |
| GitHub | `cdbb356` (Checkpoint: a1f7bcee3ab4) | No |

On GitHub, the commit `5c82fe8` points to checkpoint `02cdc0f5c85b`, but that checkpoint isn't there yet.

**Fix:** push through `origin` so the hook runs. Either of these works:
- `git push origin hello-entire-checkpoint`: the branch is already up to date, so this only triggers the hook.
- `git push origin entire/checkpoints/v1`: this pushes the checkpoint branch directly.

Your HTTPS rule doesn't really apply here anyway. Your git config has a `url.git@github.com:.insteadOf https://github.com/` rule, so Git switches HTTPS GitHub URLs to SSH. The push already went over SSH (`To github.com:migmartri/slacktronic.git`) and worked. That rule is listed about 40 times in your git config, so a setup script probably appends it on every run.
